title: Maraq Qudaar
author: Chef Amina Hassan
desc: A vegetable stew built in stages — potato and carrot first, tomato held back so they can soften, then cabbage and a mountain of spinach folded in at the end — eaten with yellow corn grits.
longDesc: In the agricultural heartland of southern Somalia, grits with vegetables was the everyday meal, while the coast leaned on fish. This is that dish: no meat, no stock unless you want it, and vegetables added in an order that has a reason behind it. The tomato comes late, because potatoes in acid take a great deal longer to soften than potatoes in water.
ingredients: 2 tsp vegetable seasoning powder, or 1 1/2 bouillon cubes
260 g (2 cups) cabbage or Brussels sprouts, quartered
240 ml (1 cup) vegetable stock (optional, if serving with grits)
375 g (5 packed cups) fresh spinach, chopped
steps: Sauté the sliced onion in the olive oil over medium heat for 2 minutes.
Add the diced potato and carrot.
Add the seasoning powder and the garlic, stir well, cover and cook for 5 minutes, stirring twice so nothing sticks.
Add the hot water, cover and cook for another 5 minutes.
Add the blended tomatoes, stir well, cover and cook for 5 minutes.
Add the cabbage or quartered sprouts, cover and cook for 5 minutes.
Add the vegetable stock now if you are serving this with grits and want it looser.
Add the chopped spinach, cover and cook for a final 5 minutes — it will collapse to a fraction of its volume.
Stir through the parsley and serve hot.
chefTips: The tomato goes in at step five, not step one. Potatoes simmered in acid stay hard for a long time, and this is the reason the stew is built in stages.
Five packed cups of spinach looks absurd going in and is about right coming out.
If Brussels sprouts taste bitter to you, quarter them and let them cook with the other vegetables — the salt and the sweetness of the carrot cover it.
Add the extra cup of stock when the stew is going over soor, so there is enough liquid to fill the well in the grits.
commonMistakes: Adding the tomatoes at the beginning, which leaves the potatoes firm however long you cook them.
Leaving the pot unstirred during the first covered five minutes, when the diced vegetables are most likely to catch.
Adding the spinach early, so it cooks to a grey sludge.
Cutting the cabbage fine — quarters hold together, shreds vanish.
reheating: Reheat gently on the hob; add water if it has tightened.
healthBenefits: Spinach is high in iron, folate and vitamins A and K.
Cabbage and Brussels sprouts supply vitamin C and glucosinolates.
High in fibre and entirely plant-based.
culturalNote: The division is geographic: in the southern farming regions people ate grits with vegetables, while coastal households relied on fish. Maraq qudaar is the inland half of that pattern, and it is what a Somali family eats on the days there is no meat.
